title: How many of your pieces are loose?
outcomes: Goes through all of own pieces without being told what to look for
Answers with a number: none, one or two or more
Separates a loose piece from one that is attacked but defended
Separates a loose piece from one that is undefended but not attacked

steps.text: In "Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?" someone told you to find the loose pieces. Now nobody does. After a move, go through **your own pieces one by one** and end with a number: how many are loose? Zero is a real answer. Remember: a piece is loose only when it is attacked **and** no piece of its own side defends it. *Undefended* (nothing guards it, even if unattacked) and *hanging* (attacked without enough defence) are related, not the same.

steps.caption: White to move. Two White pieces are loose. What happens if White does not count?

line.say: White plays a quiet move and does not count.
The pawn takes the bishop for nothing.

claims.statement: Exactly the bishop on b5 and the knight on d2 are loose.
After h3, Black wins at least a minor piece along the engine line.

steps.text: **Two look-alikes.** A piece that is attacked but defended is *not* loose, although the exchange can still go wrong (see the counting lessons). A piece that is undefended but not attacked is *not* loose either; one move can change that. Defenders count from far away, along a file or a diagonal.

steps.title: Same position, one change
steps.prompt: Count the loose White pieces in each. Predict, then check.
Think of the last piece you called safe. Which defender stood far away, and did you check that its line was open?
